initial_presentation: A 14-year-old male presented to the neurogenetics outpatient clinic in a wheelchair, with a history of progressive disabilities over eight years. He was born at full term via vaginal delivery without complications. At six years old, he developed tremors in his right hand during activities such as writing or eating. By age seven, the tremors worsened, and he exhibited a staggering gait and slow reactions. Concurrently, he experienced speech difficulties, including slurred pronunciation and slow speech. At nine years old, he developed difficulty swallowing and occasionally coughed while drinking water. His speech and coordination issues continued to deteriorate, requiring assistance for walking. At age 12, he began experiencing painful walking spasms, increased ataxia, and more severe speech difficulties, with occasional falls. He also became irritable, cried frequently, sweated excessively at the extremities, and developed urinary incontinence.

A 9-year-old girl presented with right-sided weakness and was admitted to our department around 8 hours after the onset of symptoms. She had no prior medical history, no history of surgeries, and was not on any prescribed medications. She did not report any headaches or transient ischemic symptoms. Upon arrival, her vital signs were within normal limits.

A 17-year-old girl presented with a primary concern of retained deciduous teeth. Physical examination showed short stature, prominent frontal and parietal regions, a depressed nasal bridge, a beaked nose, underdeveloped midface, an obtuse mandibular gonial angle with relative prognathism, wrinkled skin over the fingertips, and nail abnormalities. Intraoral examination identified a deep midline antero-posterior ridge of the palate, a high arched palate, multiple retained deciduous teeth with caries, crowding, and enamel hypoplasia.

An 11-year-old boy, born to first-degree consanguineous parents, was evaluated at King Abdulaziz University Hospital (KAUH) for developmental delay, cerebral palsy, and intellectual disability. Clinical assessment and history-taking determined his developmental age to be 2 months. He was bedridden with minimal distal movements and unable to attend kindergarten or school. At 15 months, he was assessed by the pediatric metabolic team for potential metabolic conditions. He was born full-term via spontaneous vaginal delivery with a birth weight of 2.7 kg and had an uneventful neonatal period. Early developmental delay and delayed milestones were noted.

The patient is a two-year-old girl born at full term to consanguineous Saudi parents via cesarean section due to breech presentation. She has a history of poor sucking, hypotonia, bilateral ptosis, and recurrent admissions to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) for apnea. The family history is unremarkable. The clinical course began with a sudden cessation of breathing lasting more than 15 minutes, followed by a three-minute arrest. She also has a history of choking and coughing. Upon examination, the patient was afebrile, dehydrated, and pale, with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 3.
A 16-year-old African American female presented with a new-onset petechial rash and palpable purpura.

A 50-year-old Caucasian male was referred to our clinic in late 2010 for elevated liver enzymes. Approximately two years before his initial visit, he experienced jaundice after taking terbinafine, which resolved on its own after three months. He reported no recent use of prescription medication, herbal medication, alcohol, or illicit drugs. There was no family history of recurrent cholestatic disorder or liver disease. Physical examination revealed marked jaundice and scleral icterus, with no signs of chronic liver disease.

A 38-year-old Caucasian woman presented in November 2017 for evaluation of secondary amenorrhea. The absence of her menstrual cycle followed the discontinuation of oral contraception, in the context of a spontaneous deep venous thrombosis (DVT) in 2015. She experienced menarche at age 13, and her menstrual cycles were regular before starting oral contraceptives. The patient had no history of infertility, having had two pregnancies and two deliveries, and reported a weight gain of approximately 4 kilograms over the past 2 years. She denied symptoms such as acne, hirsutism, or voice deepening. She had a history of high blood pressure for the past 5 years but no history of diabetes. At the initial evaluation, her medications included nebivolol/hydrochlorothiazide 5/25 mg once daily, rivaroxaban 20 mg once daily, and aceclofenac 100 mg twice daily. The patient reported progressive and persistent right hip pain that began around 4 months after her second pregnancy and persisted for 3 years, limiting her mobility.

A 3-year-old male child, born to parents who are not related by blood, presented with three slow-growing, painless, hard masses on the outer aspect of the right leg, first noticed at 2 months of age. The child was delivered at full term without any congenital abnormalities. Over time, he developed multiple asymptomatic, solid, elevated, skin-colored lesions that eventually merged into larger hard masses. The child had a history of low birth weight and delayed gross motor development milestones, but exhibited no mental retardation or gait abnormalities. There was no history of trauma, prior inflammation, or similar lesions in family members. Physical examination revealed a single large, non-tender, subcutaneous hard mass measuring 4 cm × 5 cm on the anterolateral aspect of the right thigh, with the skin over the lesion being pinchable. Additionally, there were two smaller lesions measuring 2 cm × 3 cm and 2 cm × 2 cm on the outer aspect of the right lower leg, with the surface showing atrophy and scaling. No other skeletal deformities were observed.

A 43-year-old South Asian male, with no known past medical history, presented with an eight-month history of asymptomatic, hyperpigmented patches, characterized by discrete central atrophy. The lesions were violaceous in color and ovoid in shape, appearing gradually over the dorsal aspect of hands bilaterally, and over the medial aspect of both thighs. Small multiple unilateral lesions were also noted over the lateral aspect of the right lower limb. There was no history of any recent or distant trauma, tick bites, new medication use, or any recent fungal infections reported by the patient. The patient reported that these lesions had shown the same form, texture, and color since their initial appearance, with slow and nominal growth in size noted over the course of the past eight months. Both his prior medical and familial history was deemed unremarkable. With the exception of these dermal lesions, the patient’s general health and overall physical condition were exceptional. On dermatological examination, there were two large hyperpigmented violaceous patches with atrophic changes noted on the bilateral dorsum of hands, measuring 3 x 4 cm and 4 x 6 cm in size. Small, multiple, brownish, and hyperpigmented patches with a depressed shiny center were noted over the lateral aspect of the right lower limb as well as on the medial aspect of both thighs. All patches were observed to be ovoid in shape, with a central atrophic, “cigarette paper”-like appearance, conserved pathognomonic “cliff-drop” borders, and minimal surrounding peripheral desquamation. The patient reported a lightly diminished sensation within the patches, and hence a pinprick examination was performed in and around the lesions. The sensation was deemed to be intact in all areas.
